title: VALERIUS PRESENTS HIMSELF TO THE LOCAL ELECTORAL OFFICIALS
news: Valerius follows his public declaration with the practical step of presenting himself for registration in the lowest-level civic election. He does not claim that the declaration itself gives him an office, authority, or privilege; instead, he submits his name through the ordinary local procedure available to candidates. The officials record the candidacy and identify the remaining procedural requirements before the vote can occur. Valerius accepts those requirements without attempting to substitute his military reputation or estate resources for the civic process. The announcement therefore becomes a formal candidacy rather than merely a statement of intention. No votes are cast in this round, and no electoral result is implied.

title: THE FIRST QUESTIONS OF THE CAMPAIGN ARRIVE AT THE ESTATE
news: The first direct questions from prospective local voters reach the estate after Valerius’s registration becomes known. Several ask what responsibilities he intends to assume if elected, while others ask whether his private guard and estate operations would influence his conduct in civic affairs. Valerius does not promise an office or invent powers attached to one; instead, he begins collecting the questions so that his eventual public answers can be given openly. The exchange broadens the campaign from a declaration by Valerius into an actual civic conversation. His military reputation remains part of the public discussion, but the questions increasingly concern local administration and conduct. No support total, faction, or electoral advantage is established.

title: A DISPUTE ON THE PROTECTED ROAD IS SETTLED WITHOUT VIOLENCE
news: A disagreement develops when a merchant wagon and two local carts reach a narrow section of the shared-water road at the same time. Titus Varenus sends patrolmen to separate the traffic and establish an orderly passage rather than allowing the dispute to become a contest of strength. The local travelers are permitted to continue without a toll, while the merchants are allowed to proceed once the carts have cleared the constricted ground. No weapon is drawn and no arrest is made. The incident nevertheless gives the patrols a practical test of Valerius’s instruction that protection should not become arbitrary control of the road. Both groups leave with the route still open to them.

title: THE SIXTH SURPLUS CONSIGNMENT IS SETTLED
news: The next completed delivery under the recurring surplus agreement reaches settlement during the week. Gross receipts amount to 32 denarii and operating costs to 12 denarii, producing 20 denarii of realized net public profit. The standing ten-percent routing rule transfers 2 denarii to Valerius’s private account while 18 denarii remains in the public account. The settlement is tied to the delivery actually completed and does not create a claim on future receipts. The merchants continue to use the protected road as the commercial route established by the earlier agreement. The transaction therefore strengthens an already active commercial thread without being treated as a new contract.

title: SERVILIUS FINDS A STONE MARK BESIDE THE OLDER ROADWORK
news: During the continuing survey, Publius Servilius discovers a weathered worked stone lying beside the secondary alignment. Its surface bears a partially preserved mark that appears deliberate, but the surviving portion is too incomplete to establish a name, date, or authority. Numerius Cassius records its position and leaves it in place rather than moving an object whose context may be important to the investigation. Servilius sends the observation to Valerius as evidence rather than as a conclusion. The discovery narrows the question from whether the alignment was maintained to whether surviving physical markers can identify the people or administration responsible for it. The original builder and purpose remain unresolved.

title: THE REFUGEE HOUSEHOLD BEGINS TO BECOME PART OF ESTATE LIFE
news: The refugee household admitted beneath Valerius’s shield completes its first period of settlement within the estate community. The stewards assign ordinary living responsibilities and make clear that protection does not exempt the household from the same internal rules governing other residents. The family begins contributing labor to routine estate activity rather than remaining solely dependent upon the protection that brought them there. Valerius’s principle consequently develops from an emergency act of refuge into a continuing social arrangement. No change is made to property boundaries, the guard establishment, or the authority of the stewards. The household remains protected while its place within the estate becomes increasingly ordinary.

title: CELER ACKNOWLEDGES VALERIUS’S POLITICAL ENTRY WITHOUT OFFERING A COMMITMENT
news: A further message arrives from Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer acknowledging that Valerius has entered the local electoral process. Celer does not offer an office, payment, endorsement, or formal political alliance, and Valerius does not request one. Instead, the correspondence returns to the question of how Valerius intends to separate civic responsibility from the private authority of his estate and guard. Valerius answers that the candidacy is being pursued through the ordinary civic process and that his private forces remain distinct from whatever responsibilities the office may eventually entail. The exchange leaves the relationship open and observant rather than committed. Celer’s interest therefore continues, but no political bargain is established.
